overall: The AG found no Open Meeting Law violation: the October 26 notice topic on the citizen petition was sufficiently specific, and the remaining charter, policy, process, and public-comment allegations fell outside the law and were declined.

allegations.summary: Complaint alleged the October 26 notice topic (special election petition, Article 14) was insufficiently specific.
allegations.key_passage: After review of a video recording of the Board’s October 26 meeting, we find that the notice topic was sufficiently specific.

allegations.summary: Complaint alleged portions of the Board's discussion of the citizen petition fell outside the scope of the posted notice topic.
allegations.key_passage: The Open Meeting Law does not require public bodies to list all tangential topics related to a discussion nor does the law require a public body to anticipate the course of deliberation or the outcome of a discussion

allegations.summary: Complaints alleged the Board failed to follow the Town Charter and its own policies and procedures.
allegations.key_passage: The Open Meeting Law does not, in general, govern a public body’s authority to act, nor does it govern the substance of a public body’s discussions.

allegations.summary: Complaints challenged the Board's process, its authority, and individual members' reasoning for rejecting the petition.
allegations.key_passage: Therefore, the allegations listed above, even if true, would not constitute violations of the Open Meeting Law and we decline to review them.

allegations.summary: Complaint alleged the public was not allowed to speak at the October 26 meeting.
allegations.key_passage: Likewise, to the extent the complaints allege that the public was not allowed to speak at the October 26 meeting, the Open Meeting Law does not require that a public body allow public participation

note: Read by a language model from the letter; every key passage is checked verbatim against it and dropped if not. A holding is the Attorney General’s reading of the law in this case only.
